claims.text: The target material is an as-deposited, nanoscale, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloy in thin-film or patterned-nanoribbon form.
The as-deposited films retain inherent interfacial stresses.
Interfacial strain predominantly governs the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis by modulating magneto-elastic coupling.
Limited local heat-transfer kinetics predominantly govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis.
A high-thermal-conductivity substrate or thermal-management underlayer will enhance heat transfer during magnetic-cooling cycles.
Interfacial strain and nanoscale microstructural constraints influence magneto-elastic coupling.
Interfacial strain and nanoscale microstructural constraints influence phase-transition kinetics.
Substrate-induced interfacial stresses alter magnetic-domain motion in the as-deposited films.
Substrate-induced interfacial stresses alter phase-transition behavior in the as-deposited films.
Limited heat transfer introduces thermal lag during magnetic-cooling cycles.
Enhancing thermal coupling reduces thermal lag.
Changing to a high-conductivity substrate or thermal-management layer modifies the film's strain state.
Enhanced thermal coupling and the associated strain-state change produce a more abrupt magnetic transition.
Films on a high-thermal-conductivity substrate will have a smaller hysteresis-loop width than films on a lower-conductivity substrate.
Films on a high-thermal-conductivity substrate will have a sharper and more reversible magnetocaloric response than the baseline films.
The as-deposited baseline on a lower-conductivity substrate exhibits a broader, less reversible magnetocaloric peak and significant hysteresis.
The proposed effect is expected below 100 mT, at film thicknesses of approximately 10–100 nm, and near the magnetic or structural transition temperature.
The proposed intervention is expected to matter at cycle frequencies for which thermal lag is significant.
